For some reason I found this game is more addictive than any other games I played before, include Rimworld and M&B.

It's an extremely complex Wu Xia/Kong Fu world simulator. Managing your own village, learning new style from different guides and practicing them,  finding a good partner and get married, those are just some examples from the huge amount of actions this game allows you to do.

And the story doesn't end when your character dies. Taiwu has a sophisticate inherit system, and which is actually one of the core elements in this game. It's not posible to beat the game within one or two generations.  Selecting and cultivating your inheritor carefully to make sure the next generation is stronger than the last, is a necessary and fun part of the game.

It is also a living world. In such a small game, hundreds of charactors have their own everyday life and relations just like yourself. Like in Crusader Kings, charactors don't really have very complex AI but the way the system work make you think they are alive. If you pay attention to NPCs' life, you would find many interesting storys that can be a Wuxia fiction by themselves.

The combat system is not completed yet. The current system favors those styles that causing directly injure rather than debuff. So some famous style is totally unuseable in the game(Tai Ji is a lie!!). The KongFu system is too huge to describe by simply writing about it, you would have to try to understand how it work. Let me put it in this way: it fullfill every wet dream you ever had about a world of KongFu(more precisely, WuXia).

The UI is anti-human, it must be change. Saving is not stable. Considering how much time and energy you could put on one family line, it is simply unacceptable to see your save break. 

As an early access, the developer already let us see enough potential. Thank you and please keep going. Hire a professional programmer if you can afford please, because you deserve a rest and the game deserve a better frame.
Great game. Thank you for the english translation. Been enjoying this one for many years. The recent update brought me back.

If the idea of an RPG where you wander a world filled with interpersonal NPC dynamics that are even deeper than Crusader Kings while learning martial arts, kicking ass and reincarnating across multiple generations appeals to you, this is it.

This is one of the best games in my library. It gives me the same kind of "I'll never need another game" feeling that xcom2 and rimworld gave me (though obvs it's nothing like either of them). There is so much depth in building your village and character, and progressing throughout the game, learning all the different martial arts.I'm completely hooked. (While in the meantime becoming a chess grandmaster and fathering a brood of children one of which you will probably one day be playing as).

Highly recommended.

A Warning for English Players — From a Chinese Player

If you've played Taiwu in English and felt like you were missing something you couldn't name — you were. This review is an attempt to name it.

# Part I — On Emptiness, Meditation, and a General Who Achieved Enlightenment in Battle

## The Structural Problem

Precise translation of classical Chinese is nearly impossible — not a matter of effort, but of structure. Chinese is a uniquely dense logographic language where a single character compresses millennia of layered meaning. Add classical literature, Taoist/Confucian/Buddhist philosophy, folklore, and ancient medical concepts, and accurate translation becomes structurally impossible. Historical attempts to render the *Zhuangzi* or *Dao De Jing* into English have always fallen short — not from lack of skill, but because the target language lacks the equipment to receive what the source is transmitting. A game localization team under commercial deadlines never stood a chance.

This gap has deep roots. Western engagement with Chinese thought has historically followed material interest, not intellectual curiosity — from the silk trade to Marco Polo to Enlightenment philosophers like Voltaire and Leibniz, who idealized China as a rational meritocracy. Then the 19th century arrived: industrial power, colonial expansion. The admiration collapsed. Western perception has always swung like a pendulum between romanticization, arrogance, and strategic wariness — and the translations that survived each swing reflect that.

## 虚室生白 — The Emptied Vessel

Zhuangzi gives us the most precise description of what meditation preparation feels like in four characters: **虚室生白** (*xū shì shēng bái*) — *empty, room, generate, white/brightness.*

The "room" is the mind. "Emptied" is an active discipline — deliberate subtraction, the clearing of mental clutter. "White" is not brightness but clarity: the quality of awareness that arises when you stop filling the space with noise. My translation: ***"The emptied vessel illuminates."***

*Vessel* earns its place because the Western tradition carries the same intuition from the opposite direction. Paul's "earthen vessels" (*2 Corinthians 4:7*) hold divine light precisely *because* they are hollow. The theological concept of *kenosis* — God self-emptying to take human form — runs on identical logic: reduction enables illumination. Two traditions, thousands of miles apart, arriving at the same paradox.

This is not poetry. It is a description of a preparatory state — the condition you enter before meditation begins.

## Qi Arts: You Already Know This Practice

Qi Arts (气功/内功) is the internal cultivation underlying every impossible feat in the game. What the localization never tells you: **it is meditation.** Literally.

The same practice appears across every major civilization under different names. The *hesychasm* of Orthodox monks, the *contemplatio* of Catholic mystics, Sufi breathwork, Buddhist *samatha* and *vipassana*, Confucian *jìngzuò* (静坐, quiet sitting), Taoist *zuòwàng* (坐忘, sitting in forgetting). Every traditional Chinese medical student still receives formal meditation training in college — the practitioner's inner stillness is a clinical instrument, not a spiritual hobby.

The 20th century repackaged it commercially: Mindfulness, MBSR, Google's Search Inside Yourself, Flow State coaching, the Wim Hof Method. The branding changed. The mechanism did not.

## Wang Yangming and the Battlefield Test

**Wang Yangming (王阳明, 1472–1529)** — neo-Confucian philosopher, military strategist, battlefield commander — pushed this tradition to its operational limit. He argued, and *proved under fire*, that the highest internal stillness is not achieved in a quiet room. It emerges when the inner mind is completely calm while the outer world is in absolute chaos. Later, people called this 心学 (*Xinxue*, Heart-and-Mind Learning).

Psychologists today call it **Flow State**. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi arrived there through decades of research with rock climbers and chess grandmasters. Wang Yangming arrived there in the 15th century through philosophy and battlefield command. Same phenomenon. Five centuries apart.

The chain runs from 虚室生白 — empty the vessel — through every monastery, medical college, and corporate mindfulness retreat in history, to a general who used the resulting stillness as a military asset. When your character sits cross-legged in Taiwu to cultivate Qi, they are participating in something humans across every culture have practiced for thousands of years. The English translation gives you a fantasy mechanic. The Chinese original is pointing at something real.

---

# Part II — The Game Review

## Depth — ★★★★☆

**Pro:** Exceptional systemic complexity — martial arts, relationships, cultivation, craftsmanship, medicine, and time, all layered and genuinely interactive.

**Con:** Scope creep produces decision fatigue. True freedom requires mods. Hunyuan Qi builds are frustratingly difficult to maintain.

## Freedom — ★★★☆☆

**Pro:** Genuinely permissive — bandit roleplay, NPC murder, polyamory, high-tier crafting at low cultivation. The simulation lets you become who you choose.

**Con:** A rigid ceiling hides beneath the freedom. High-tier martial arts require massive grinding or cooking mastery (which requires its own grind). Combat is hard-capped by cultivation level. Primary attributes cannot be trained organically. Seriously — give the character a pair of dumbbells and enough protein.

## Cultural Depth — ★★★★★ (Chinese) / ★★☆☆☆ (English)

**Pro:** For native Chinese speakers, the game is intuitively legible and deeply rewarding. Everything hums at the right frequency.

**Con:** The localization frequently undermines the experience. Three specific failures:

**奇门武器** → "Exotic Weapons." Should be "Unconventional" or "Unorthodox Weapons." The point is tactical heterodoxy, not cultural foreignness.

**鸳鸯连环脚** → "Feet of the Mandarin Duck." In Chinese, mandarin ducks symbolize perfect pairing — elegant. In English, it sounds like a menu item. "Linked Double Kick" or "Swan Double Kick" (swans also mate for life) would land far better.

**元山弹腿** → "Yuanshan Tan Tui," untranslated and unexplained. "Tan Tui" (弹腿) is a real, historically documented Springing Leg system — foundational northern Chinese martial arts. Without context, it reads as a random placeholder.

## Combat — ★★★☆☆

**Pro:** Tactical dungeon crawler with genuine micro-decision density. Qi functions like mana — the genre conventions work within their own logic.

**Con:** Strictly 1v1, making teammates ornamental. Instrument-based martial arts are overpowered — they should fail against anyone deaf or wearing ear protection. More broadly: Chinese armies used firearms from the 10th century. If martial arts fail, bullets finish the job. At minimum, add crossbows. In a pure 1v1 meta, a bandit with a pouch of quicklime defeats every grandmaster in the game.

---

## Final Verdict

Accept the design loopholes (shared by most wuxia games) and tolerate the translation failures with enough patience to puzzle through the gaps — this is a genuinely excellent game.

Otherwise: **keep your money for extra chicken wings and soda water.**

*— A Chinese player who has spent too long thinking about four-character phrases*

After spending a significant amount of time with Scroll of Taiwu, researching the game's systems through both the in-game wiki and extensive Chinese guides and forum discussions, I've come away disappointed by how little substance there is beneath its enormous surface.

At first glance, Scroll of Taiwu appears to be a deep sandbox cultivation RPG filled with complex systems, faction politics, character relationships, crafting, management, and martial arts. In practice, almost all of those systems ultimately exist to support one goal: preparing for a sequence of eight boss fights.

The game's progression loop quickly reveals itself. Identify the next boss, determine its weaknesses, then either build specifically to exploit those weaknesses or simply accumulate enough stats to overpower it. Nearly everything else in the game exists only as a means to facilitate that process.

The biggest issue is that very little side content feels worthwhile. Most activities consume valuable time while offering rewards that can usually be acquired more efficiently through other methods. Once you understand the mechanics, much of the game devolves into an end-turn simulator where you're simply waiting for resources, relationships, or training progress to accumulate.

Unfortunately, the combat doesn't carry the experience either. Compared to games like Tale of Immortal, combat feels relatively uninteresting and lacks the excitement needed to justify the amount of preparation leading up to it. Since the boss fights are the primary destination of the entire progression system, this leaves the game without a compelling payoff.

The problem becomes even more apparent when examining the game's individual systems.

Martial arts acquisition initially appears flexible and immersive, but in reality it's largely deterministic. Need a specific technique? Go to the sect that teaches it, befriend a sufficiently skilled member, and learn everything you need. There's little discovery, experimentation, or meaningful uncertainty involved. Once you know where the abilities are located, acquiring them becomes routine.

Itemization suffers from a similar issue. Crafting eventually boils down to creating exactly the item you want. Materials are generally straightforward to obtain through harvesting, trading, or NPC interactions, meaning gear progression lacks the excitement of adapting to unexpected finds or making difficult choices.

Town management sounds like a major strategic feature, but in practice it mostly functions as a money and prestige printer. Rather than presenting interesting management decisions, it primarily serves as another mechanism for obtaining resources needed elsewhere.

The NPC system is perhaps the most disappointing of all. Relationships rarely feel organic or engaging. Instead, social interactions often amount to repeatedly challenging characters or sharing random pieces of information until they like you enough to provide whatever benefit you're seeking. For a game that places so much emphasis on its living world, the characters themselves feel remarkably mechanical.

What ultimately surprised me most is that Scroll of Taiwu's greatest strength should have been its systems. The game presents itself as a complex simulation where numerous mechanics interact in interesting ways. Instead, most systems are shallow, deterministic, and exist largely in isolation. Once you understand the optimal path, much of the mystery disappears and the experience becomes surprisingly linear.

In the end, I found it to be an extremely lackluster experience and one that I would struggle to recommend over the many stronger cultivation and wuxia games currently available.

If you're struggling to find the translation (as it starts in chinese), either click the dropdown box in the top left (marked by an icon with a circle) or select the third box down in the menu to access settings and change it in the dropdown there. With the official english translation the game is more accessible than ever, but english speakers will likely still run into a bit of cross-cultural barrier as far as the actual contents of the text still. There is however very little like Scroll of Taiwu that's accessible to an english audience, so if you're willing to bear with the confusion of stepping into Wuxia/Xianxia stuff, I fully recommend it, as it's worth the time and is quite deep with a lot of moving systems.

It is still a very complex game, so you will need to be patient, do the tutorial/look up information like you would stepping into a game like Crusader Kings for the first time. There's a couple pieces that they seem to have missed in the translation, but nothing that impedes understanding so far.

但是600小时之后你问我我的游戏感受，我认真的回答你：枯燥，但是不无聊。快乐，但是不轻松。

这游戏的重复性是否存在，认真地说存在，大多数游戏都存在的重复性在这个游戏中体现的可能更为明显一点。但是无论是地鼠（侠客）风云传还是刨矿世界（Minecraft）这种哪怕是半开放世界的游戏，重复性工作都是客观存在的。只是这个游戏采用了更极端的方式：它不再是点一下一个动画告诉你你学习了某个武功，而是采用了两个纯数字硬核游戏来表达你读书（心法）和练功（突破）的过程。这两个游戏硬核到很多玩家根本无法接受其中的数学模型，只是觉得：我做不到。实际上，游戏中遭遇战斗胜利过后会提高战斗突破的基础成功率，较艺胜利过后会提高杂学突破成功率。读书更是可以凭借堆悟性，造藏书阁阅经阁等多种手段来打成目的。但是唯一的问题是……看头顶上我说的前三句话。游戏开发者很清晰的表达出了，你想成为武侠中的人上人，你就需要付出足够的努力。你需要读书，练武，不同的武功还需要不同的技艺支持（比如少林寺的武功你需要佛学很好，然山仙师的武功就要求你在占卜上投入更多的精力）。也许可能会门口一个乞丐在机缘巧合下学会了太极剑法，但是由于他没有剑术基础，也没有道法理论支撑，个人资质没有定力加强。虽然剑法使出来凭借剑法的精妙能打到我。但是伤害效果却是大打折扣。完全符合越高深的武功越难的逻辑————但是也有特例，比如狮相门是个纯外功门派，它的武功就只要求你体格足够强悍，身体越好攻击就是越高。
可是以上的一切，体现在几十个小时的游戏逻辑里，你会发现你就真真正正的成了一个江湖中人。你需要真的拿出江湖中人应有的时间去练武。台上一分钟，台下十年功的含义被表现得淋漓尽致。武侠小说里我们看到的都是快意恩仇，却很少有人思索在快意恩仇背后，每一个侠客背后所付出的艰辛努力。

这也就是这游戏差评的由来：是我们玩游戏，还是游戏玩我们？我们代入了游戏中的人物，却发现我们不由自主的被这个江湖所控制，本来生活就很累，玩个游戏难道也要这么累么？

但是这也同样是这个游戏好评的由来：这就是真实的江湖，真正的武侠游戏，没有付出就是没有回报。也许五代人的努力，可能仅仅是为了最后一剑定乾坤的舒爽，是在无尽的默默努力之后终于得到回报的畅快。

我通关3个周目了，但是依然乐此不疲。虽然，真的很疲……

但是……我依然乐在其中，因为天知道这个档会变成什么样子……这个档里的世界会变成什么样子。我喜欢在通关的过程中，认真的去读每一个跟我有交集和没有交集的NPC随机出现的故事。被妖女蛊惑，千夫所指的少林方丈；一心爱慕百花谷谷主，最终做好事做到誉满天下的五仙教圣姑；村中行乞，机缘巧合偷学会一招太极剑法后干脆拜入武当，终成一代名宿的小卒。不甘被棒打鸳鸯，和被金刚门驱逐的弟子一同跑去村庄做木匠的少妇。心性大变入魔的人，就算你解救回村子，他的仇人依然会不死不休的追逐，除非你这个村长出面消耗声望来化解。因为萍水相逢爱慕你的人，也可能这辈子不求名分的跟你东奔西走（哪怕不在一个队伍里）。

你可以做一个优秀的村长，村庄科教文卫繁荣昌盛，各地商贾慕名而来，岁入近百万银钱（哪怕是最顶尖的材料书籍不过十万银钱），天下事没有钱砸不下来的。你也可以做一个行侠仗义的侠客，学好武功仗剑天涯，装备全靠杀歹徒强盗爆，钱全靠卖东西所得，浪迹天涯四海为家结交天下英雄。你还可以当个江湖大盗，专挑名门大派的弟子下手，杀其人，夺其谱。你甚至可以当个天下第一厨神，路边采个鸡蛋做一盘天地一口香，天下英豪会为之驻足……问题是……你做哪一个，都需要付出足够的努力。赚钱你就要安排人手建设村子，调配人工世界各地找材料，必要时候甚至要亲自跑去买，同时还要研究对应的技艺（譬如你想修藏经阁，那么你佛学至少要达到相当高的造诣），如果你要出去行侠仗义，你至少一半的时间是闷在家里读书练功的，否则你就不是去行侠仗义，而是被行侠仗义了……而这个过程的枯燥，和你最后获得的快感，成不成比例……只能说见仁见智吧……

扯了这么多没用的，最后说一句，这是个好游戏，我会一直支持下去。不推荐没时间的玩家选择这个游戏，它真的一点都不快餐，甚至认真地说你的第一次成就感可能甚至来自于100小时之后回顾这个过程的努力……

但是无论如何，武侠就在这里，太吾就在这里……

The Scroll of Taiwu is definitely one of the best independent rougelike games I’ve ever played, and it’s my most anticipated strategy RPG in near future.
The game is based on an ancient Chinese Wuxia world-set, but perhaps borrowed some concepts of Chthulhu which makes it an interesting mix: There is a threatening being known as Xiangshu (相枢), which slowly corrupt people’s mind and once nearly destroyed the whole world. And the characters you play are the successor of Taiwu (太吾), who hold a Saint Sword (伏虞剑) and are supposed to stop Xiangshu and save the world. The work will continue for generations, so after the first character dies (get killed or just reach his/her age), you’ll play his/her successor, who could either be the son/daughter, or a companion you had (your decision to make). The skill you learnt will be passed on by the Saint Sword, but because each character has his/her unique status which may or may not be suitable for the build you planned, you should plan very carefully before making decision about the successor of your current character.
The game is a turn-based sandbox RPG, similar to Taiko Rissiden, you spend your action point practicing skill, visiting different places for adventure, or collecting your resources to build your base (Taiwu Village). After all your action points spent, you enter the next month and may encounter random events depending on what you did and who is standing next to you. There are two different types of skill trees: one is fighting skill and the other one is your life skill, for both skills, you need to collect relevant skill books to learn, and practice/breakthrough in an appropriate building (both require your action point). In current version, there are 15 factions in the game where you can learn different skills, but you can only learn the very basic ones at the beginning until you earn enough support from other members in the faction to unlock the next tire. Furthermore, ‘learning’ the martial art (fighting skill) is merely the very first step, in order to master each skill you also need to meet different requirements, which can be a life skill, or your character stats (by the way, you do not simply gain exp and ‘level up’ in this game, you only get a higher stat by ‘equip’ a skill you learnt)
I’m not going too deep to the complex fighting mechanics, which may worth a whole wiki site to explain, and I’m going to list a couple of other things you might find interesting:
1.	Completely random but interesting interactions between npc: all NPCs in this game live their own life (or even next-life) which may or may not has anything to do with you. They fall in love, get married and have a family, become enemy or best buddy with other NPCs. Although there isn’t much lines they speak (which may because this game is still in Beta version), but it makes you feel that each character has a unique personality and life. 
2.	Beautiful but somewhat realistic Martial art combat display: finally, the martial art skill is no longer one slash followed by a beam of laser or something. I also believe each fighting skill has a unique animation.
3.	Cricket Fight: You gotta catch 'em all!
As I said a number of times, this is still an early access version so the game still have a number of things need to be improved: NPC’s AI and their action is a bit too random and sometimes seems ‘very wrong’, the content in late game might be a little repetitive, the game only automatically save after each term and sometimes you have to be a save-scum to roll the best results. And most importantly, this game only has Chinese sub at this moment and probably for a while. But please understand and give the develop team just a little more time (considering it only has 4 formal members in the team up to this point, and believe or not, they are basically self-funded during the process of developing), there will be a masterpiece in one or two years.

[h3]Introduction[/h3]
This is a highly replayable mythological-wuxia sandbox combat-oriented RPG with extensive relationship simulation in a story generator, with base-building element.

[h3]The English Translation[/h3]
	While the developers announced that English translation is part of their plan, we are still very far away from its implementation. The language used in the game is written in Classical Chinese. The dev reported 4 million words in the game. New tutorials and in-game wiki are planned. With two more sects and three main storyline updates in the queue, I speculate that the English translation is impossible until mid-2026.
The dev announced that they have started working on the translation in Apr 2025 live stream. They also planned to have monthly major updates, with five or less updates before 1.0.

[h3]The Game Story[/h3]
	The player is the Chosen One who can eliminate the world's evil. The game's background is in the fantasy realm of China, around 1000 AD. The world's inhabitants are tormented by a demonic presence named Xiang Xu. When the NPCs or the player experienced a prolonged depression, they would be possessed by Xiang Xu. Possession by Xiang Xu is a death sentence. The player, named Taiwu, is the only one in the world who can exorcise possessed individuals, making him a savior. Only one Taiwu can exist in the world at a given time. All major sects made a pact with Taiwu to teach their moves. In return, Taiwu will travel the world to eliminate Xiang Xu. Learning one move months in-game time and is impossible to learn all the moves in one lifetime. Fortunately, Taiwu also owns the hilt of a broken legendary sword called Fuyu, which allows Taiwu to transfer all his knowledge and experience into the sword. The following person who inherits the sword will be the next Taiwu, picking up all the knowledge from the previous Taiwu.

[h3]The Game Mechanics[/h3]
	The [b]reversed designs[/b] contributes to its steep learning curve. The developers attempt to be innovative by reversing many game mechanics familiar to RPG players. For example, in a typical RPG, the depletion of an HP bar usually means death or defeat. The HP bar in this game is better understood as injury markers, which implies death or defeat when full.
	
	The game attempts to [b]gatekeep the progression[/b], resulting in uneven pacing and waste of time. Obtaining better quality items, powerful moves, or high social status NPCs are locked behind defeating dungeon bosses. Defeating the dungeon bosses will progress the state of the world, making Xiang Xu more rampant. However, defeating regular enemies becomes a nuisance when the player becomes powerful in the endgame. The frequent enemies spawn on the world map make combat a mind-numbing chore. Multiple major game mechanics are also locked behind the game progression, such as the reincarnation system, the kung fu competition, the establishment of the Silk Road, the emergence of the heavenly books, etc.
	
	The unintuitive [b]book reading[/b] is one of the major criticisms of this game. To learn a move, the player must master the theoretical and practical aspects of the move. The theoretical element can be mastered by reading the relevant book. Each book will come with a summary, five chapters, and varying conditions. The entire book-reading gameplay, including the hunting and reading all the book chapters, is boring.
	
	This is [b]not a stream-friendly game[/b]. The interactions between NPCs, with or without the player's interference, made the world lively. However, the interactions are only presented in texts, which requires the players to fill in the gap with their imagination. The dungeon crawling aspect is just hex-tiles map, with confusing markings, reducing its appeal (planned for overhaul in the future).

[h3]The Combat[/h3]
	The combat is always in [b]1v1, 2D side-scrolling format[/b]. Pausing in the middle of the combat is allowed for precision control. All other NPCs in the party act as supportive characters. The player may learn the combat moves from the 15 sects in the world, each with unique 40+ moves. Every move comes in two opposites; for example, Shaolin's long fist deals [i]external[/i] injury when learned from reading a positively written book, whereas the same Shaolin long fist deals [i]internal[/i] injury when learned from a negatively written book. Combined with the different game mechanics, such as five types of poison and 14 types of weapons, the players can dream up infinite builds. All bosses and enemies have their own fighting styles, making boss fights a real challenge. A single-boss fight is usually a showcase of all the experiences accumulated over several lifetimes; winning it is deeply satisfying. However, battles with regular enemies are frequent and mind-numbing, which are usually skipped with the auto-combat feature.

[h3]The Developers and the Mixed Reviews[/h3]
	The developers are notorious for refusing to accept and listen to the community’s feedback. The community has pushed for the release of the main storyline for years, but the developers refused. Instead, they chose to revamp the minor systems related to the sects in the game world since mid-2019. To the community's dismay, the developers decided to go into close beta in mid-2020, only releasing sporadic news in between until they re-release the revamped version in late-2022. The community felt cheated as the game was riddled with game-breaking bugs and was severely under-developed, resulting in a mixed review.
	
	The developers’ stubbornness turned out to be one of their greatest strengths. While the community constantly doubted the developers, they stayed true to their visions and continuously updated the game. Hopefully, their dedication will prove the doubters wrong and recover from the undeserving mixed review.

[h3]The Story Generator[/h3]
	This game has a lively world, a perfect game for master storytellers. Hundreds of NPCs are spawned during the creation of the game world, each with its unique name, personality, likes and dislikes, social roles, belongings, knowledge, etc. These NPCs may grow up, fall in love, get married, have children, and die of old age on the other side of the world without the player's intervention. The NPCs may develop a crush, get rejected, harbor resentment, exact revenge, lose their belongings, be harmed in natural disasters, or get injured or poisoned. They may not even have the chance to meet with Taiwu in person before death, only to be discovered decades later when Taiwu passes by their tombs.

[h3]The Relationship Simulator[/h3]
	While the game system only allows monogamous matrimony (re-marry is possible after the death of spouse), it is possible to build a harem with lovers and concubines. Rape, incest/inbreeding, extra-marital affairs, family trees, genetics, LGBT, fertility, physical attractiveness, the birth of twins and triplets, and birth defect are all possible in this game, allowing complex storytelling. The behaviors of the NPCs are tied to their morality. Evil-aligned NPCs are more likely to engage in obscene acts. Leaving your spouse behind to travel the world (traveling across the map takes months, and training takes years), it is not uncommon to find your spouse has given birth to several children upon your return. Jealousy and rivalry between romantic interests may even lead to duel or murder. 

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
If the Chinese gaming community were to describe this game in one word, it would be “[b]hardcore[/b]”. You will probably spend around 100+ hours before reaching the final boss. The current game also has a lot of game breaking bugs, with even more game breaking bugs introduced in each major update. If game breaking bugs is a deal breaker, potential buyers may withhold until 1.0 release. This game is a masterpiece, but it is not a game for everyone and definitely not a game for casual players. The main storyline is still a work in progress.

Ok now It's been 58hours in game. I didn't spend much time on the game bc I busy working life but tbh I'd rather spend all my night playing this game, but if I do that I'll die. Now this is a game that I spent a lot of hours and completed all achievements but still couldn't recommend to any one.  There's a slim chance that a very niche group of players who are extremely patient, love unconventional complex systems and a lot of interest in Chinese culture may appreciate the game.  But there are still way too many issues for me to recommend.  

The learning curve of the game is very steep.  From the character building, equipments, combat system to interactions between characters,  almost all systems are unconventional and complex.  It will take a lot of effort to understand the system and to come out with a viable strategy.  I strongly recommend new players to play on the easiest difficulty.  Even on the normal difficulty, most players will suffer a lot.

As if the learning curve is not steep enough, AI chatbot is useless to this game, as 90% of the time AI chatbots will give you outdated guides and information.  The game is patched frequently and the mechanism can be changed often.  Due to this, most of the mods are not useable if not updated recently.  One of the most terrible things can happen is your save file with 200 hours get corrupted due to a latest patch conflicting with mods.  

The story is disappointing.  I have little interest to meddle in deities' business especially when I don't like either side.  All those deities are just selfish childs that inflicting pains to mortals.  Being tricked to work for them and without a choice is just frustrating.  

The user interface is terrible, as many players have mentioned.  The game is released on Huawei Phones and the UI has been changed to cater for the phone version's needs.  There are many functions difficult to find or not easy to see.  E.g. I only found the manual book reading function after 100 hours of game time.  There're several functions I only discovered at the late stage of the game, although I have been reading the in game wiki diligently. 

The game could be interesting for awhile when constructing viable builds, but it's getting repetitive quickly and switching builds are quite painful.  Regional quests and main stories are quite long, and more than half of the game is grinding mindlessly.  Interesting interactions between NPCs seems to be greatly reduced than earlier versions.

Achievements are mostly achieveable in one run.  On easy difficulty, one full run of finishing all books, all quests and all endings (with manual back up of saves) will take about 300 - 400 hours.  On higher difficulties, the time required could easier go above 500 hours. 

8 years ago, I played this for awhile and it had a promising future at that time.  It's quite unfortunate that the game ended this way.

Whilst I have enjoyed the actual gameplay so far, the utter lack of any manual save system makes this game a chore to play. With its dense systems with so many interconnected parts and a vibrant world to explore it would be an incredibly fun time if you had the ability to save your progress mid month as taking the time to read and understand the systems takes time and real life can get in the way of playing whilst you are halfway through a month. I am sure that with practice and understanding a lot of the decisions and gameplay can be progressed through quickly enough that experienced players can manage just fine but for new players or even those who cannot have long play sessions the lack of ability to save and pick up from where you left off is crippling to the initial onboarding of the game and means I cannot recommend it.

I hope in future there will be some patch to allow manual saving.

EA玩家，本来想等1.0再给真正的review，但是这么多年过去了，我觉得再等可能我要挺不过这个游戏了。

其实游戏的优点很多，对武侠文化的精准把握，出色的世界概念，和庞大的内容，都能看出诚意。但是，有一个老生常谈的问题——游戏，终究是拿来玩的。

很明显茄子对于武侠很有想法，但是对于如何让玩家获得乐趣，就毫无头绪。
1.奇遇
整个游戏的核心循环其实就是如何获取更强的功法，然后通过组合和练度，战胜更强的敌人。在早一些的版本中，甚至整个家园建造的终极目的，就是为了能获取高阶人物的喜爱度，并且想办法得到/修复/修炼他们的秘籍。而在这样的一个世界中，你会惊奇的发现，练就一身神功的你，并没有什么特别的地方可供探索。
整个奇遇设计简直是逆着整个行业而行，毫无任何互动，唯一的互动是路线安排，而路线安排又不能直接选择，而是有一套几乎没有任何其它系统会用到的’赋性‘来决定，除了个别情况可以稍微更改路线，玩家几乎毫无控制能力，只能被动服从安排。在杀戮尖塔和黑暗地牢的同一时代，你很难想象竟然有这样的设计，从’教你玩游戏‘，直接进入了’你看设计师玩‘这样的离奇境界。
而且格子的所有奖励，都要考验技艺水平。这本身无可厚非，但是这又是一个没有互动环节，实际上一次奇遇，除了打架意外，其他的格子都没有任何互动。而且，更令人发指的是，在玩家开始游戏不久，’古墓仙人‘这一必做奇遇，已经开始要求150点的技艺水平。注意，这时玩家根本没有任何精纯，甚至没有加入门派，没有任何人可以可靠的指点出150点的技艺。那你设置这个不切实际的要求有什么意义呢？只会让玩家养成忽视格子的习惯。
综上所述，这个游戏的所有地下城，走到哪你控制不了，而格子之间也没什么本质差别，除了打架（大地图上也有的是人可以挑战）几乎不提供任何其他内容，反而通过一系列的被动灌输拖慢节奏。以至于有了’直接打奇遇boss‘这类mod，打了之后游戏体验还成倍增长。可见关卡设计，如果这个游戏真的有的话，已经差到什么地步。

2. 敌人和boss设计，其实整个游戏最有趣的地方，就是想进各种办法跳精纯拿到神功，配出想要的功法。面对某个难解的敌人的时候，总有那么几种特别的功夫，能够让你反制住强大的对手，从而提供成就感。
可是敌人的强大真的有必要到这种地步么？掐时间放护体，掐距离放催破，有些敌人还会放三个小弟来回出来挡刀，而且boss的护体几乎都是没有破绽的，放出来就要老老实实等它结束。
而如此精明的敌人，在极长的版本更替中，又常年被卡武器距离导致一刀放不出，被逆狮子吼一个功法删除了所有护体甚至催迫技能，甚至有些版本中，boss甚至会反复猛攻玩家的护体，导致自己杀死自己。全程突出一个智障，和神经病。
这里出现了一个很奇怪的现象，茄子对战斗的设计是完全按照玩家博弈的思路来的，AI不是配合玩家玩游戏，而是把自己当成玩家。很明显的对比是，杀戮尖塔，boss几乎都是循规蹈矩按照一个固定模式行动，但是就是好玩，你也不觉得它笨——因为任何一个人都已经知道，这是AI，它的强大来自于它的超模数值和特殊机制，而不是因为AI很聪明。
对于现代游戏来讲，搞清楚这个boss的机制，凑出足够多的属性，就可以顺利成章的打赢。而不是搞出一个一方面很聪明，一方面又很傻的AI，让玩家寻找这个AI那些地方有思维死角，那些机制AI没理解或者不会应对，这样不是更好的玩法么？
实际上很多boss本身的设计也的确是如此，找对防御属性，找对护体和绝技，通过正常手段获胜是最爽的。可是茄子总是怕boss不够强，非要搞出一系列的测dps机制，逆天的回复，加上大量的无限叠加性属性，搞得本该正常获胜的战斗，经常由于一个疏忽，让boss放出一个护体，或者拖过了时间，就前功尽弃，然后读档，再走一遍又臭又长的剑冢迷宫，用同样的战术重新打。
有必要这样设计么？现代游戏的设计思路是让玩家赢，却没那么容易赢，而不是让敌人设计和AI尽量想办法卡住玩家。

3. 没有章法，故弄玄虚和不知所谓的机制。
有多少人在大地图上反复追一个紫竹化身，结果好不容易找到，人家跳地图了。交换了半天藏书，结果一个门派凑不出一本正的高品功法，甚至低品功法都凑不出来。生孩子个个东倒西歪，还经常给我反目成仇，真的有必要么？
还有以秘闻为首的一系列边缘机制，你说有用，偶尔有用，但你说完全不用，游戏照样玩。立意非常好，可是真的有必要这样设计么，看了秘闻找不着人，找到了人用不上，好不容易用上一次，也是形式大于内容。而相比之下，去非人峰和少林寺搞私奔的剧情要有趣不知道多少倍。那你为什么要花时间死磕秘闻，而不是再多搞一些门派内，非主线的奇遇呢？
还有那个十世转生，我顶你个肺阿，让人好好玩游戏就有那么难么？你是做游戏做出幻觉，感觉自己是所有人的人生导师了是么？我呸！
4. 不完善的奇怪UI。那个反选武功filter我就不说了，建筑界面，到了今天，都还不能去掉无法建造的建筑，我真的不知道这个公司有没有UX和QA。

总之，这个游戏现在还勉强保持着独一份的武侠世界和内容广度。但是在各色中文沙盒游戏层出不穷的今天，我，一个EA起就一直在关注太吾的老玩家，真的已经挤不出一丝丝的动力再打开绘卷。就以这篇review，作为饯别的信物。阿叔我终究没能等到茄子写完这个故事，江湖路远，有缘再见。

Pros:

- The world feels alive since NPCs live their own lives like the protagonist sans the village management.
- Unbelievable amount of skills and kung-fus to learn and master, and this is where you would spend time on the most(unless you are into cricket fighting)
- The music is nice, but could be better.
- Relationships between characters can go very wrong, be prepared for pedophiles and CK2-esque idiosyncrasies.

Cons:

- Newborn infants seem to know more types of kung-fus than you do, and they can sometimes even be the leader of a sect.

IMO Most people are morally ambiguous, and there are no good guys or bad guys, there are only people who did the right thing at the right time and people who did the wrong thing at the wrong time. I’ve noticed a lot of the negative reviews from new players seem to come from a mismatch in expectations. Once you understand what *The Scroll of Taiwu* is actually trying to be, many of those concerns become a lot less severe.

This is not really a “main character” RPG. Your starting character is not *the* protagonist. The focus is your lineage, your sect, and the long-term legacy you build over time. The monthly save system can definitely feel frustrating at first, especially when you think you’ve lost progress, but it makes more sense once you realize the game is built around continuation rather than one perfect character run.

I’m new to Wuxia-style games, and the Chinese gaming scene is still pretty new to me, so there has been some culture shock. I’ve restarted a few times because certain mechanics were unclear, and I do think the game could explain some systems better. That criticism is fair.

That said, the in-game lookup tool, community guides, and Discord have been extremely helpful. Once it clicks that this is more about managing your lineage and martial clan’s future than protecting your first character forever, it becomes a deeply rewarding experience.

**TL;DR:** Great game, but a lot of the frustration comes from misconceptions about what type of experience it is. It’s not a main-character RPG; it’s about lineage, legacy, and building your martial clan over time. Some mechanics are confusing, and that criticism is understandable, but putting a little effort into learning what you don’t understand makes the game much better.

第一次经历太吾绘卷，觉得那就像是一部精彩的小说，有角色，剧本，背景设定，画面，机制。就仿佛真的如同天地的绘卷般，梦与江湖的宏大在挥毫泼墨间展现得淋漓尽致。

但当你真正开始游玩时，你就发现体验完全不是这么一回事。有多少的时间浪费在了查找攻略，寻求Build，搞最优解，种田，SL读书。新手或者一般的玩家要么缺乏指引，要么没有时间去专研，根本没有能力去参与这些曲折离奇的伤害计算机制，或者学习研究游戏的内容。而当你真正花时间去研究了之后，发现也许来来去去的也就是一些偷窃流，种田流，核弹流这种既成的套路。而等你真的天下无敌之后，你又会觉得后期的游戏内容乏善可陈，除了主线以外，并没有什么别的可做了。而主线本身，又充满了作者自身个人的喜好，作为小说看也许还行，但作为游戏的一部分意义不大。

这就好比你为了玩这个游戏，必须去做大量和玩游戏无关的内容，仅仅只是为了玩好这个游戏，而当你发现你真的玩好了这个游戏之后，这个游戏就已经没什么可以玩的了。

沙盒游戏的乐趣本来就在游戏的自由度，对未知的探索，对世界的发掘，和NPC的交流，资源的采集和利用。但是练武的时间却大大占用了这些游戏当中原本该是核心的部分。玩家被迫在探索和习武之间选择，必然就会造成设计和体验间严重的割裂。而如果游戏的最终目的仅仅只是为了挑战剑冢，那么开放世界的意义又何在呢？为了找一个外表随机得不错的NPC当伴侣？为了体验一下各种乱搞性关系的节目内容？离开了直播间的节目效果和论坛的话题，又有多少人会孜孜不倦地反复去做这些事情呢？


我能感受到螺舟在太吾绘卷的创作中倾注的满满诚意，但却又不得不说游戏的机制和设定上实在是有太多这种似是而非的东西。

缺乏以游戏体验为中心的设计逻辑，使得太吾绘卷能够打破常规，大胆创新，发展出新的沉浸式体验，但却终究逃脱种种机制流于表面，不合常理，以及昂杂无用的问题。过于零碎，割裂，以及不能相辅相成的游戏内容，令我甚至觉得螺舟不是在做一款游戏，而是在写一部小说的同时做一款迷你小游戏，你只有在小游戏上通关了，才能把这本小说读下去。

虽然这么说了，但我觉得太吾绘卷还是国产游戏的一次了不起的创新，一款独一无二的作品。我希望螺舟工作室能够一直努力下去，我期望能够见到他们的下一部作品。

Thank you dev team, it's been a long wait.

Steep Learning Curve: Because the game offers so much content and freedom, the sheer volume of systems can feel overwhelming at first. If you don't like digging into mechanics, you might find it tedious or frustrating. But if you’re someone who loves exploring and learning deep systems, this will feel more like a huge plus than a minus.

Summary:

Update: After playing the (nearly) full release for a while I feel I can comment on the changes. To begin with: nothing in the new game's systems are worse then the previous ones. We've lost some things that are familiar (I personally loved the old reading system), but the systems that replace them either have more depth or more accessibility. Often both. This is still the same familiar game that everyone fell in love with, and the developers have shown their passion with daily bug fixes and updates. Which leads into my second point.

What's the most different about the update? The performance. I don't think people realise just how poorly optimised the previous version of this game was. It was horrendous, and it would get increasingly worse the more turns you took in the game. I was looking at upwards of 5 minute loading times for each turn on a gaming rig that can play the latest releases in 4K Ultra. Because it wasn't a hardware limitation but a software. The new version is incredible in comparison and it's obvious how much effort was spent in the backend of the game during closed development. That alone is an incredible difference.

Why is the game not released yet? The game needs lots of QA work. Bug fixing. Many minor improvements that really need to be worked on. The developers have always sucked at prioritising QA and the game's only just getting the bare-bones of its much needed QA now. Part of the reason you see people getting mad in the reviews is because there are no real tutorials. The game's still not new-player friendly.

People getting upset at the game is justified. Their blatant attempt at misleading people who read their reviews isn't. The update is a strong step forward for the game regardless of what they personally believe. Is it worth getting now? Yes, especially if you want to take advantage of EA price. The fan English translation is very presentable right now, and the official one will release in 3-6 months. The content is all there - balance, bug-fixing and QA are the core of the updates. However you can also wait. At this pace you're looking at them finishing off the game's polish in the same ETA as the translation (3-6 months).

I have always loved Chinese wuxia stories, but this game completely failed to live up to my expectations. After nearly 500 hours, I came to the realization that this is a terrible game—just as I once came to the realization, far too late, that my ex-boyfriend was a terrible person.

1. There is no Japanese localization. I had to choose between reading English at a painfully slow pace or reading Chinese, where I could only understand about half of the content.

2. There is no manual save system. As a result, I frequently lost my progress.

3. The game provides very little guidance for new players. The in-game encyclopedia does not solve this problem; if anything, it makes things even more confusing. While this did not affect me personally, I still consider it a serious design flaw.

4. As for the gameplay, it appears to offer a great deal of freedom on the surface. In reality, however, it feels as if the developer prepared nine specific problems for the player to solve. Each of these problems has both a general solution and several specific solutions. If you discover the general solution, the rest of the game becomes little more than gathering the required resources, waiting for long periods of time, and eventually reaching the ending while trying to follow a story that is often difficult to understand.

5. Regarding the art style, I do not personally like it, but it is at least distinctive. I would say it is barely acceptable.

In conclusion, I regret purchasing this game. It wasted both my money and my time.

I never played early access and am an english speaker, however I have played other esoteric chinese martial arts games like amazing cultivation simulator and tale of immortal. 

Right now I am playing on hard difficulty and I am still in probably the early/mid game of this game and I'll give you a breakdown of what to expect. So far I am finding this game to be really fun, though extremely complex with a lot of complex mechanics that I am still trying to figure out how to min/max.

This by its heart is a stat min/maxing game where you try to find synergies between all the martial arts to make a god like character. there are like 15 sects in this game and each sect has like 50-100 martial arts, and each martial art has unique effects. the martial arts are ranked from tier 9(weakest) to tier 1 (strongest), however when you breakthrough each martial art you can get an unique effect, the effect can either be blue or red and can be build defining (some passive, some active). Because of the unique effect, some Tier 9 (weakest) martial arts you will use till the end game because they synergize well with other stronger martial arts, so every tier of martial arts can be viable in the end. The build possibilities are honestly kind of crazy, like its not too hard to make a decent build you just learn all the martial arts of one sect and make a build with just one sects martial arts, but you can wrack your brain trying to piece together a min max build because you are not constrained to learning the martial arts of just one sect.

As for the sandbox portion of the game, story wise there is a main story and I think you can pursue a few endings to the main story but at the beginning you are doing the same things in terms of main story, and each sect has their own extensive side story quest that each give end game rewards. The true sandbox part is how you interact with the NPCs to get what you want, you can steal/swindle or learn martial arts legitimately to make your build. There is even a super in depth crafting system where you can min/max your gear but I haven't dabbled in that yet despite my dozens and dozens of hours.

You can recruit NPCs and assign them "jobs" like you and literally make a NPC companion a vendor of a specific type so you have a portable vendor with you at all times. Sandbox wise there are tons of tons of things you can do, but however if you are expecting to make your own main story then yeah this is not the type of game.

If what I described sounds fun then get this game, I personally am having a blast. However if you are expecting some kind of build your own main story with 1000 branching randomly generated storylines or something (does any game actually do that?) then this is not the game for you, like the first few hours of the game you will always end up being the mayor of a town, but thats literally is just the tutorial (1% of the game), the game just opens up from there, you can decide to take on fighting the bosses of the sword mounds or just run around doing whatever, making friends, joining sects and learning their martial arts or whatever and ignore the sword mount bosses until you are ready.

Oh and crickets are OP, you can get learn up to tier 3 martial arts even in the early game by beating high level characters in cricket duels in the early game. This is a mixed opinion, really. The game is complex, with a very interesting topic and idea (nurturing your martial artist characters through generations, making them powerful enough to challenge an ancient evil, and in the meanwhile interacting with a living wuxia world complete with cricket fights, poetry tournaments, ancient martial arts manuals, rivalries and romance and fights to the death). It is quite idiosyncratic and peculiar in how it does various things, the interface is very much cluttered, the gameplay can feel like it lacks a direction or like you are living a real martial artist's life, and - most importantly for me - the English translation is the worst official English translation I have ever seen in any game. Heck, fan-translated wuxia novels are leagues better. It is just enough to get by, but a lot of nuance and detail gets lost.

I give it a thumbs up as an encouragement, if the translation doesn't improve I'll have to switch the review to negative.
just misses the cultivation vibe for me, gating power behind bosses that require specific builds is just a wild choice imo.

Anyways, now that the release version of the game is out, I do have to say the changes overall has gone in the right direction,  and for the most part makes the game more fun, and leave me with high hopes for the future development. I can still see it as Taiwu but alot also changed and had to be relearned. Overall though, the QoL of the game has been imrpoved compared to the atrocious original, art got all around better, and the new combat/martial art/book reading system all seems to be taking things in the right direction.

Make no mistake however, this game is still a game in its EA stage, I have beat 3 of the sword tombs and content isn't significantly improved from old taiwu, just polished or redone. Some of the new addition like the chicken house and multiple travel locations doesnt seem to do much at all. There are many janky balance issues like cricket battle now bringing almost no income (was too high before), you can pretty easily cheese the art competition to rob NPC of items without making too many enemies, etc... But the dev have done a good job in the last few days pumping out updates, if it keeps up, I am optimistic.

As for bugs people mentioned, I have not encountered anything game breaking that can't be fixed by simply exit and restart, but fortunately I am following the path of those who came before as dev seems to be fixing bugs that appear just a tad ahead of my progress. 

Lastly, just like the original taiwu, the ingame tutorial and info is atrocious and will not help you learn the game at all, if you cannot watch a chinese guide video I'd suggest wait until some more guide comes out, even now I am half trying to figure out mechanics, half searching on baidu as I go.

Overall, you traded one EA game with massive potential with a more polished EA game with massive potential, but very much still an EA game. I dont see it leaving EA for awhile, so if you can wait, I'd suggest you do, but if you really want to scratch the taiwu itch after the long hiatus I'd say you will have fun as you always had with the previous version.
